title: Exploring the Impact of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Thematic Analysis
extended_summary:
This paper examines educator perspectives on generative AI in education, asking what advantages, limitations, and practical challenges are perceived when tools such as ChatGPT, Bard, and Bing AI are introduced into teaching and assessment. Rather than testing a specific intervention experimentally, the authors conduct a thematic analysis of seven opinion essays written by educators and supplement this with exploratory text analysis.

The study focuses on educators from higher education, with participants teaching subjects including machine learning, programming, databases, distributed systems, statistics, digital marketing, game development, and research methods. The context is primarily tertiary education in Ireland, with one contributor affiliated with an institution in India. The paper discusses how educators view GenAI as a tool for boilerplate generation, troubleshooting, personalized support, and prompt-based assistance, but also as a source of academic integrity concerns, hallucinations, plagiarism risk, over-reliance, and reduced independent thinking.

The main conclusion is that educators see both promise and risk in GenAI. They support responsible integration through prompt instruction, human oversight, and updated assessment methods such as authentic/project-based/oral assessment. The paper does not provide comparative outcome evidence on whether GenAI improves teacher planning or feedback relative to human coaches or standard supports; instead, it offers a qualitative synthesis of educator opinions about broader educational uses and risks of GenAI.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative thematic analysis of seven educator opinion essays, not an intervention evaluation. It does not use a controlled design, comparative outcome measurement, or inferential statistics to estimate causal effects.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper offers useful descriptive insights about how educators perceive GenAI’s impact on teaching and assessment, but it does not provide measurable evidence of effect sizes or demonstrated outcomes. Its practical impact is therefore indirect and mainly informative for policy and future study design.

interventions.use_case: Thematic analysis of educator opinions about ChatGPT, Bard, Bing AI, and similar large language models as educational tools for tutoring, coding help, prompt-driven assistance, and classroom use.
Discussion of GenAI used to provide feedback on student work, including code troubleshooting, partial code correction, and support for revised outputs.
Discussion of LLMs as tools for text generation, essay drafting, summarization, citation/reference generation, and general writing support in education.

finding.finding_summary: Across 7 educator essays, the paper finds widespread concern that GenAI complicates academic integrity, assessment design, and institutional policy. Educators repeatedly argue that current plagiarism-detection and LLM-detection tools are insufficient and that institutions need updated policies, authentic assessment formats, and clearer guidance for staff and students. No effect size is reported because this is a qualitative thematic analysis rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: Qualitative thematic analysis of educator essays; themes related to academic integrity, assessment policy, and institutional guidance

finding.finding_summary: Educators describe both gains and losses for higher-order skills. On the positive side, GenAI can support troubleshooting and independent progress in coding tasks; on the negative side, over-reliance may reduce problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity, and independent judgment. No quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of educator comments on problem-solving, creativity, independent thinking, and student independence

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI may improve efficiency by automating boilerplate tasks, generating templates, producing minimal working examples, and helping students resolve coding issues faster. At the same time, educators caution that superficial copying and unverified outputs can create downstream inefficiency when work must be corrected or rechecked. No quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of time-saving, boilerplate generation, debugging support, and reduced need for immediate human assistance
